opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think skepticism is healthy, and I'd probably be skeptical too if I were on the outside. What we're trying to do is hard, and it doesn't fit neatly into the current mainstream narrative. Right now a lot of people believe the path forward is mostly about scaling language models: more data, more compute, bigger models. If you hold that view, then anyone betting on a different direction looks either naive or contrarian for its own sake.

But I don't think of it as being contrarian. As a researcher, I've seen many times that what everyone takes for granted in one period gets revisited a few years later. Ideas that seemed dead come back, and things that seemed obviously right turn out to be only part of the picture. My own sense is that real intelligence has to be grounded in the world, in seeing, in understanding space and physics, in learning from experience, not only from text. That's a conviction built on years of working on vision and representation learning, not something I came up with to sound different.

So when people don't believe in us, I don't spend much energy arguing. Debates in AI usually aren't settled by talking; they're settled by results. Our job is to build things, publish, ship, and let the work speak. If we're wrong, we'll learn that quickly and adjust. If we're right, the skepticism will fade on its own.

And there's another side. If everyone already believed in what you're doing, it probably wouldn't be worth doing, because someone else would already be doing it with far more resources. Being doubted is part of the price of working on something non-consensus. I'm okay with paying it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses skepticism broadly but does not identify a divide between Silicon Valley and the rest of the world.

r002.rationale: It says debates are settled by results, that the work should speak for itself, and that skepticism will fade if the company is right, conveying that skeptics should wait to see how the path turns out.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask skeptics to decide whether to join him or commit to his chosen path.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think skepticism is healthy, and I don't take it personally. If everyone immediately believed in what you're doing, that would probably mean you're doing something too obvious, something that the big labs will just do next quarter anyway.

I come from a research background, so I'm used to this. When we were working on ConvNeXt, a lot of people had already decided that convolutions were dead and transformers were the only future. When we worked on diffusion transformers, people asked why we were bothering, since the U-Net already worked fine. In both cases, the right response wasn't to argue harder. It was to run the experiments carefully, show the results, and let people update on their own. I think the same applies to a company.

The second thing I'd say is that a lot of the doubt is actually reasonable, and I try to separate the parts that are reasonable from the parts that are just noise. People say, you're a researcher, you've never built a product. That's fair. People say the frontier labs have more compute and more data than you. Also fair. But I think there's a confusion between the scale of a problem and the direction of a problem. A lot of what's valuable in AI right now isn't just more scale on the same recipe. It's figuring out what the next recipe should be. And that's exactly where a small, focused team with good research taste can move faster than a very large organization that's optimizing an existing thing.

I also think about this in terms of time horizons. If you look at vision, at representation learning, at how we're still really bad at having models understand the physical world, these are not problems that get solved in six months. So when someone says, I don't see how this becomes a business in a year, I kind of agree with them. That's not the bet. The bet is that this matters a lot over five or ten years, and that the people who understand the fundamentals will be the ones who get there.

And finally, I'd just say, I'd rather be doubted and be working on something I genuinely believe is important than be universally approved of and working on something incremental. Doubt keeps you honest. It forces you to be very clear about what you actually know, what you're guessing, and what you still need to prove. For a researcher that's a very familiar and, I think, very good place to be.

astra-6.text: I think it’s fair to be skeptical. When you’re trying to build something new, you can’t expect everyone to share your conviction from the beginning. I’d want to understand why they don’t believe in it. Is there a weakness we’re overlooking? Is there something we haven’t explained clearly? That feedback can be useful. But ultimately, we have to build something that works and let the results earn people’s trust.

sol-6.1.text: I think skepticism is natural, especially when you’re trying to do something ambitious. I’d listen carefully and ask what specifically they don’t believe in. Sometimes there’s useful feedback there. But ultimately, we have to earn people’s confidence through what we build and whether it works. I’d rather focus on making progress than trying to convince everyone upfront.
